lead: A pushdown automaton finishes a run when its input is used up. At that moment two different conditions can declare success: the machine sits in a final state, or its stack is empty. Both are called acceptance, and each defines a language. This chapter gives both definitions and shows that each kind of machine can be rebuilt to work like the other, so the two families of languages are exactly the same. Only a few universities teach this as its own topic, but the construction is used whenever a PDA has to be turned into a grammar.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for the seven-tuple, the move relation ⊢ and instantaneous descriptions.

blocks.text: The seven-tuple P = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, Z₀, F) comes from 4.1. A run starts at (q₀, w, Z₀): start state, whole input, stack holding only the bottom marker. The run ends when the input is empty. Two different end conditions count as success.
Final state acceptance. The machine must be in a state of F when the input runs out; the stack may still hold anything.
L(P) = { w ∈ Σ* | (q₀, w, Z₀) ⊢* (q, ε, γ), q ∈ F }
blocks.where: Σ* is all strings over the input alphabet; ⊢* means zero or more moves; ε is the empty string; γ is whatever stack contents remain.

blocks.text: Empty stack acceptance, also called acceptance by null stack or by empty store. Here the state is irrelevant; the stack must be bare.
L(P) = { w ∈ Σ* | (q₀, w, Z₀) ⊢* (q, ε, ε), q ∈ Q }
blocks.where: Q is the full state set, so any state will do; ε as the third entry means the stack is empty.

blocks.text: The two rules look like different machines. They are not. Each can be simulated by the other, so both accept exactly the same languages.
Final state to empty stack. Given P with final set F, build P′. Keep Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀ and Z₀ as they are.

items: Choose a symbol X₀ not in Γ. It is the new bottom marker.
Add a start state q₀′ with δ(q₀′, ε, X₀) = {(q₀, Z₀X₀)}.
Add an erasing state qe. For each q ∈ F and each Y ∈ Γ ∪ {X₀}, put (qe, ε) in δ(q, ε, Y).
Set δ(qe, ε, Y) = {(qe, ε)} for every such Y.

blocks.text: Once the old machine sits in a final state with the input finished, step 4 hands control to qe. The eraser pops one symbol per move until nothing is left. The new machine copies each move of the old one, so it accepts the same strings, now by empty stack. Its final set can be empty.
Empty stack to final state. Given P that accepts by empty stack, build P″. Keep Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀ and Z₀.

items: Choose X₀ not in Γ and add a start state q₀′ with δ(q₀′, ε, X₀) = {(q₀, Z₀X₀)}.
Add one final state qf, and for every state q ∈ Q add (qf, ε) to δ(q, ε, X₀).

blocks.text: X₀ reaches the top only after the old machine has emptied its own stack, so the jump to qf fires exactly then. Again the new machine copies each move of the old one. This equality of power is what lets 4.4 choose whichever rule is convenient.

figure.caption: The new start q₀′ puts Z₀ on top of a fresh bottom X₀ and hands over to the old machine; when the old machine reaches its final state q₂, the eraser qe pops everything. On aabb the stack goes Z₀X₀, then X₀, then empty, so aabb is accepted by empty stack.

spec.aria: Top: q₀′ leads into the old PDA q₀, q₁, q₂, and q₂ leads to an eraser state qe that loops popping any symbol. Bottom: the stack on aabb, X₀, Z₀X₀, Z₀X₀ at q₂, X₀ at qe, then empty.

examples.question: The PDA of 4.1 has Q = {q₀, q₁, q₂}, Γ = {Z₀, A}, start state q₀, bottom marker Z₀, F = {q₂}, and it accepts aabb ending in the ID (q₂, ε, Z₀). Apply the final-state-to-empty-stack construction and trace aabb on the new machine.
steps: New bottom marker X₀, not in Γ. New stack alphabet: {X₀, Z₀, A}. New states: q₀′, q₀, q₁, q₂, qe.
δ(q₀′, ε, X₀) = {(q₀, Z₀X₀)}, so Z₀ sits above X₀ and the old machine sees its usual bottom.
For each Y in {X₀, Z₀, A}: δ(q₂, ε, Y) = {(qe, ε)}. Only q₂ is final, so only q₂ gets these moves.
For each Y in {X₀, Z₀, A}: δ(qe, ε, Y) = {(qe, ε)}. The eraser pops one symbol per move.
All old moves are kept. The new final set is empty.
Trace: (q₀′, aabb, X₀) ⊢ (q₀, aabb, Z₀X₀) ⊢* (q₂, ε, Z₀X₀) ⊢ (qe, ε, X₀) ⊢ (qe, ε, ε).
examples.answer: The run ends at (qe, ε, ε), so aabb is accepted by empty stack even though the new machine has no final states.

traps: Taking X₀ from Γ. If the marker was already in the stack alphabet, the old machine could push or pop it and its own runs would change.
Adding erase moves out of non-final states. The eraser may start only after the old machine has finished, or the machine accepts prefixes it should reject.
In the other direction, forgetting the guard: jumping to qf whenever some symbol sits on top. Only X₀ says the old stack is empty.
Mixing the rules. 'Accept when in a final state and the stack is empty' is a third, stricter condition that neither standard definition uses.

quiz.q: State the condition for w to be accepted by final state.
quiz.a: (q₀, w, Z₀) ⊢* (q, ε, γ) for some q ∈ F and some γ ∈ Γ*.

quiz.q: State the condition for acceptance by empty stack.
quiz.a: (q₀, w, Z₀) ⊢* (q, ε, ε) for some q ∈ Q; the state does not matter.

quiz.q: Why must the new bottom marker X₀ be outside Γ?
quiz.a: The old machine's moves are defined only for symbols in Γ. If X₀ were in Γ, the simulated machine could push or pop it and its behaviour would change.

quiz.q: After the final-state-to-empty-stack construction, which moves leave a final state q of the old machine?
quiz.a: For every Y ∈ Γ ∪ {X₀}, the move (q, ε, Y) → (qe, ε), one symbol popped per move. No input is read.

quiz.q: Give the first two IDs of the converted machine on input aabb.
quiz.a: (q₀′, aabb, X₀) ⊢ (q₀, aabb, Z₀X₀). The new start pushes Z₀ above X₀, then the old machine runs.

quiz.q: The converted machine has F = ∅. Why does it still accept the same language?
quiz.a: Acceptance here is by empty stack, which ignores the state. After the old final state, the eraser pops every symbol down to ε, so every old accepting run becomes an empty-stack run.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real parsers do not run a literal PDA; they compile the moves into a table and use an array as the stack, so a parser stack overflow is a genuine bug class. Pushdown systems also appear in software model checking, where a program's call stack is abstracted as a pushdown store and reachability stays decidable. Search for 'pushdown system reachability' or 'P-automata' to go further.
